cases.grading_notes: States that the sketching approach uses a human-written sketch, while Learning to Infer Program Sketches uses a learned neural sketch generator to produce sketches from specifications before symbolic search.

results.question: How do The Sketching Approach to Program Synthesis and Learning to Infer Program Sketches differ in how program sketches are produced?
results.answer:
They differ in **who/what produces the sketch and whether it is fixed or learned**.

- In **The Sketching Approach to Program Synthesis**, the sketch is **provided manually by the programmer**: “*one manually provides a sketch of the program to be induced*” and “*a complete sketch is a StreamIt program P that implements some permutation f*” [DBLP_conf_pldi_Solar-LezamaRBE05_page_8]. The sketching compiler then uses that programmer-written sketch as a constraint on synthesis [DBLP_conf_pldi_Solar-LezamaRBE05_page_8].

- In **Learning to Infer Program Sketches**, the sketch is **generated by a neural network and learned from data**. The paper says the system has “*a sketch generator, and a program synthesizer*,” and the sketch generator is “*a distribution over program sketches given the spec*” that is “*parametrized by a recurrent neural network*” [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_3]. It is trained so the network “*learn[s] how much to rely on each component of the system*” and can output sketches “*without explicit supervision*” [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_2][DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_3].

So, in short: **Solar-Lezama et al. use manually written sketches; Nye et al. learn to produce sketches automatically from specifications** [DBLP_conf_pldi_Solar-LezamaRBE05_page_8][DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_3].

results.question: How do The Sketching Approach to Program Synthesis and Learning to Infer Program Sketches differ in how program sketches are produced?
results.answer:
The papers differ in whether sketches are **hand-specified by the programmer** or **learned by a model**.

- In **The Sketching Approach to Program Synthesis**, sketching is a programmer-driven process: “the programmer uses partial programs to describe the desired implementation strategy” and “leaves the low-level details … to an automated synthesis procedure.” The paper says a “complete sketch is a StreamIt program P” and that “the programmer actually writes the simpler proper sketch” in their examples. So sketches are produced manually as partial programs or rewrite-rule-like constraints. [DBLP_conf_aplas_Solar-Lezama09_page_1]

- In **Learning to Infer Program Sketches**, sketches are produced by a learned sketch generator: the system has “a sketch generator, and a program synthesizer,” and the generator is “a distribution over program sketches given the spec: qφ(sketch|X).” It says the generator is “parametrized by a recurrent neural network,” and the system is trained “to assign high probability to sketches” that help synthesis succeed. So sketches are inferred from specs by a neural model rather than written by the user. [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1902-06349_page_3] [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1902-06349_page_2]

In short: **Solar-Lezama 2009 uses human-authored sketches; the later paper learns to infer sketches automatically from specifications.** [DBLP_conf_aplas_Solar-Lezama09_page_1] [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1902-06349_page_2]

results.question: How do The Sketching Approach to Program Synthesis and Learning to Infer Program Sketches differ in how program sketches are produced?
results.answer:
They differ in **who/what produces the sketches and how flexible that process is**.

- In **_The Sketching Approach to Program Synthesis_**, the **programmer writes the sketch directly** as a partial program, leaving low-level details unspecified: “the programmer uses partial programs to describe the desired implementation strategy, and leaves the low-level details … to an automated synthesis procedure” [DBLP_conf_aplas_Solar-Lezama09_page_1]. The paper also says the programmer provides “a sketch—a partial program” plus a specification such as tests or a reference implementation [DBLP_conf_aplas_Solar-Lezama09_page_1].  
- In **_Learning to Infer Program Sketches_**, the sketches are **learned/generated automatically by a neural sketch generator** from the specification: “Our system consists of two main components: 1) a sketch generator, and 2) a program synthesizer,” and “The sketch generator is a distribution over program sketches given the spec” [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_3]. The paper emphasizes that the system “learn[s] how much to rely on each component” and can output either more complete or more general sketches depending on difficulty [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_2][DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_3].

So, **Solar-Lezama 2009 uses programmer-authored sketches**, while **Nye et al. 2019 learns to infer sketches from specs automatically** [DBLP_conf_aplas_Solar-Lezama09_page_1][DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_2][DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_3].

results.question: What evidence does Learning to Infer Program Sketches provide about the benefits and limitations of automatically inferred sketches?
results.answer:
The document says the system’s inferred sketches help because they let the model “dynamically incorporate pattern recognition and reasoning,” and the learned intermediate representation “allow[s] a program synthesis system to learn, without direct supervision, when to rely on pattern recognition and when to perform symbolic search.” It also says the model “matches the memorization and generalization performance of neural synthesis and symbolic search, respectively,” and “outperforms existing models on several programming tasks.” [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_1]

The document does not provide evidence about limitations of automatically inferred sketches beyond implying that different parts of the problem require different mechanisms; it does not explicitly discuss failure cases or disadvantages of inferred sketches. [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_1]

results.question: What evidence does Learning to Infer Program Sketches provide about the benefits and limitations of automatically inferred sketches?
results.answer:
The paper argues that automatically inferred sketches are beneficial because they let the system “learn how much to rely on each component” and “flexibly learn the optimal amount of detail needed in the sketches” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1902-06349_page_3]. It also says that using sketches as an intermediate representation and training them self-supervised “allows our model to increase data efﬁciency and generalize better to out-of-sample test tasks compared to RNN-based models” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1902-06349_page_2].

It also gives evidence about limitations and tradeoffs: when a task is easy or familiar, the system should output “very complete sketches,” but when a program is “unfamiliar or difﬁcult,” the sketches should be “very general, so that the synthesizer must do most of the computation” [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1902-06349_page_3]. More generally, the paper says the division of labor between sketch generation and symbolic filling is not fixed, and the system must adapt to the task difficulty and available search budget [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1902-06349_page_2][DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1902-06349_page_3].

A concrete example of the benefit is that the model can produce sketches with some holes and the synthesizer can fill them in, as shown in the text-editing examples where the sketch leaves certain tokens as `<HOLE>` and the corresponding hole fillers are inferred [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1902-06349_page_15]. 

So, in short: the evidence is that inferred sketches improve flexibility, efficiency, and generalization, but they are not uniformly detailed; their usefulness depends on whether the task is easy or hard, because harder tasks require more symbolic search to fill more general sketches [DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1902-06349_page_2][DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1902-06349_page_3].

results.question: What evidence does Learning to Infer Program Sketches provide about the benefits and limitations of automatically inferred sketches?
results.answer:
The paper provides several pieces of evidence that automatically inferred sketches are beneficial because they let the system adaptively split work between neural recognition and symbolic search.

- It says the model “**learns to find good intermediates between pattern recognition and symbolic reasoning components**” and “**outperforms existing models on several programming tasks**” [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_1].
- The key claimed advantage is flexibility: unlike previous systems with fixed sketch grammars, this approach can “**learn how much to rely on each component of the system**” and “**output a more detailed sketch**” when the task is easy or a “**more general sketch**” when the task is difficult [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_2].
- The training scheme is designed so that the generator produces sketches that can be synthesized within a sampled time budget, meaning the system learns “**the easiest sketch which still solves the task within that timeout**” [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_5].

Evidence of benefits from the experiments:
- On list processing, SKETCHADAPT “**requires much less enumeration to achieve high accuracy**” than the synthesizer-only baseline and “**far exceed[s]**” the generator-only model on harder out-of-sample programs [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_6].
- On string editing, “**SKETCHADAPT outperforms the ‘Synthesizer only’ model**” and “**matches or exceeds**” the generator-only RNN model [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_7].
- On AlgoLisp, the system “**considerably outperforms baselines in the low-data regime**” [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_7].

The paper also gives evidence of limitations:
- A generator-only RNN “**performs very poorly on the out-of-sample length 4 programs**,” showing that inference-by-pattern alone is not enough for harder generalization settings [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_6].
- The synthesizer-only model can benefit from a large enumeration budget, but it “**does not take advantage of learned patterns**” and therefore is less efficient on easier programs [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_7].
- The authors note that performance of the generator-only model is sensitive to beam size, while SKETCHADAPT is “**less dependent on beam size**,” suggesting sketches help stabilize search [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_7].

In short, the paper argues that automatically inferred sketches are useful because they can make synthesis more efficient and improve generalization, but the evidence also shows that sketches are most valuable when they help balance recognition and search; neither pure neural generation nor pure enumeration is sufficient on its own [DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_2][DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_6][DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19_page_7].
